candidate.educational_objective: Counsel a long-term older smoker that tobacco cessation remains an effective cancer-risk-reduction intervention regardless of age or smoking duration and should not be replaced by screening alone.

options.A: Quitting now still lowers your risk of smoking-related cancers and other diseases; benefits occur even after many years of smoking, so cessation support is still worthwhile.
options.B: You are correct; cancer risk no longer changes once a person has smoked for several decades.
options.C: Quitting is useful only for people younger than 40 because older adults do not gain meaningful health benefit from cessation.
options.D: Continuing to smoke is reasonable if you undergo cancer screening because screening eliminates the additional cancer risk from ongoing tobacco exposure.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. CDC states that quitting smoking lowers the risk for multiple cancers and that this benefit applies regardless of age, how long a person has smoked, or how much the person has smoked. NCI likewise states that people who quit smoking, regardless of age, reduce their risk of smoking-related disease and cancer compared with people who continue to smoke. B and C are incorrect because cessation benefit is not restricted to short-term or younger smokers. D is incorrect because cancer screening does not neutralize the carcinogenic effects of continued tobacco exposure; cessation and appropriate screening address different aspects of risk and prevention.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Smoking causes multiple cancers; quitting reduces cancer risk compared with continued smoking; meaningful benefit remains regardless of age and after long smoking duration.

candidate.stem: A 62-year-old client who has smoked cigarettes for more than 30 years says, 'There is no point in quitting now because the cancer damage is already done.' Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
